partner_context.their_ambition: The Ministry of Transport is building a modern, integrated network across land, sea and air — the Doha Metro and Lusail Tram are running, and the Water Taxi project has already delivered its first terminals at Lusail, The Pearl and the Corniche. The 2050 Transport Master Plan sets out a national water network from Al Wakrah to Al Khor across eight stations on three lines, all tied together through the Sila public-transport system.
partner_context.their_pressure: Doha's growth rings a compact, traffic-dense bay — West Bay, Lusail, The Pearl, Katara, the Old Doha Port — where the straight line between two points is across the water, not around it. Qatar is committed to a 25% cut in emissions by 2030 under Qatar National Vision 2030, and the Ministry has stated an eco-friendly, modern water-transport goal for the project.
partner_context.where_navier_fits: The Ministry has built the terminals — with electric-charging pontoons — and is still selecting the operator and the vessels. Navier is the vessel choice that makes the national water network fast and zero-emission from day one: near-silent, low-wake foiling boats that run in more weather and reach the whole coast, integrated with the Metro, the tram and the bus network through Sila.

hero.eyebrow: Authority proposal · State of Qatar · Ministry of Transport
hero.title: A national water-transport network for Qatar
hero.subtitle: Qatar has already built the water-taxi terminals and published the network — Al Wakrah to Al Khor. Navier is the zero-emission, foiling fleet that makes it fast across Doha Bay and the whole coast.

why_now: Qatar's coast is a compact, water-first geography — Lusail, West Bay, The Pearl, Katara, the Old Doha Port, the airport, Al Wakrah and the northern towns all face the same sheltered Gulf water, yet most trips between them still loop along congested roads. The Ministry completed the first water-taxi terminals at Lusail, The Pearl and the Corniche in November 2024 — built with electric-charging pontoons — and published a national network from Al Wakrah to Al Khor. The operator and the vessels are still being chosen. This is the moment to make that network a fast, near-silent, zero-emission foiling service.
multimodal_fit: The water layer is national transport infrastructure, not a ride-hail add-on. It plugs into the Doha Metro, the Lusail Tram and the bus network at shared interchanges, shares ticketing and journey planning through the Sila public-transport system the Ministry is already standing up, and gives the airport a direct waterside arrival. Every route adds capacity to the public network without adding a car to Doha's roads.

journeys_unlocked.today: A short bay trip that still loops along congested West Bay and Lusail roads at peak.
journeys_unlocked.with_navier: The live water-taxi core, foiling-upgraded — quicker, quieter and running in more weather.

journeys_unlocked.with_navier: A direct, all-electric hop across Doha Bay between two of the three live stations.

journeys_unlocked.today: A road trip to the airport, congested at peaks.
journeys_unlocked.with_navier: A waterside airport transfer straight from the Doha core, bypassing road traffic.

journeys_unlocked.today: A coastal road run south to Al Wakrah.
journeys_unlocked.with_navier: A direct foiling link down the sheltered east coast to the southern terminus.

differentiation.headline: Built for public value
differentiation.body: This proposal is measured the way a ministry measures transport: trips shifted off congested roads, emissions avoided against the 2030 target, airport and coastal access widened, and the waterfront and tourism better served. It is a public network running on infrastructure Qatar has already built — with a credible operating model, not a marketplace.

proof_points.claim: The Ministry of Transport completed the first water-taxi terminals — Lusail, The Pearl and the Corniche — in November 2024, with electric-charging pontoons.
proof_points.evidence: Lusail Ferry Terminal (>2,200 sq m), Pearl Ferry Stop and Corniche Ferry Stop; operator and vessel type selection underway.

proof_points.claim: Qatar's 2050 Transport Master Plan sets out a national water network from Al Wakrah to Al Khor — eight stations on three lines.
proof_points.evidence: Connecting Doha, Lusail, Hamad International Airport, Doha Port, West Bay, The Pearl and Simaisma.

proof_points.claim: A direct Qatar–Bahrain passenger ferry opened in November 2025 — the first direct sea route in the Gulf.
proof_points.evidence: Al-Ruwais (Qatar) ↔ Sa'ada Marina (Bahrain), 70–80 minutes; booking via the Masar app.

proof_points.claim: Qatar targets a 25% cut in greenhouse-gas emissions by 2030; a zero-emission marine mode contributes directly.
proof_points.evidence: Qatar National Environment and Climate Change Strategy; Qatar National Vision 2030.

objections.q: Is this proven, or a novelty?
objections.a: Qatar has already built the terminals and a Qatar–Bahrain ferry now runs. Navier is the fast, clean fleet that runs on infrastructure the Ministry has built — quicker and able to run in more weather than a conventional ferry.

No. The first routes use the completed Lusail, Pearl and Corniche terminals — whose pontoons already have electric chargers — and the marinas and jetties along the coast. The network grows from what is already built.

objections.q: How does it fit the rest of public transport?
objections.a: It connects to the Metro, the tram and the bus network at shared interchanges and shares ticketing through the Sila system. It adds capacity without adding cars to Doha's roads.
Around public value — emissions avoided, congestion relieved, access widened — plus a transparent operating model. The exact fares, frequencies and cost-recovery are set with the Ministry.

the_ask: Partner with Navier on a feasibility study: run the completed water-taxi terminals with zero-emission foiling vessels, map the full Al Wakrah-to-Al Khor network with the Ministry, and scope an optional cross-Gulf link to Bahrain — all integrated with the Sila system and the wider transport plan.
close: Qatar has already built the terminals and published the network. Navier turns that into a fast, clean, national water service — Doha Bay and the domestic coast first, the cross-Gulf link when the State is ready.

why_navier_now.step_change: Hydrofoiling is a genuine step-change in speed, comfort, wake and noise over conventional ferries — enough to make scheduled water transport a serious everyday mode across Doha Bay, not a harbour cruise.
why_navier_now.no_new_infrastructure: The first routes use what already exists: the completed Lusail, Pearl and Corniche terminals — whose pontoons are already fitted with electric chargers — and the marinas and jetties along the coast. No new roads or land take are needed to start.
why_navier_now.the_moment: The terminals are built, the Metro and tram are running, and a direct Qatar–Bahrain passenger ferry opened in November 2025. Water transport is already part of the Ministry's plan and its charging-ready infrastructure — this is the moment to choose the fast, clean fleet that runs on it.

levers: Navier is not introducing a novelty. MOT has already built water-taxi terminals with electric-charging pontoons and published a national network from Al Wakrah to Al Khor. Navier is the vessel choice that makes that network fast and zero-emission from day one: foiling hulls are quicker, near-silent, low-wake, weather-resilient and longer-range than conventional displacement ferries — enough to serve the dense Doha Bay core, the airport and Al Wakrah, the northern coastal extension, and a credible cross-Gulf relief corridor.
A zero-emission marine transport mode contributes directly to the 25%-by-2030 GHG target and to the eco-friendly public-transport goals MOT has stated for the Water Taxi project.
